# Before You Try to Go Deep

Sometimes going deeper is the wrong move. If you're so far inside the frightened kid that pausing, comparing two options, staying in the room, or doing what you had decided to do is getting hard, don't force a deep dialogue just because this is an inner-child guide. Get more support around you first. The conversation can wait.

[EXISTING BOTTOM-UP HEALING EMBED — UNCHANGED]

## You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue

This guide also doesn't require a running voice in your head. Some people think in words almost constantly and some barely do. Can you choose to think a sentence silently even when sentences don't usually arrive on their own? That's a different question. So is whether a feeling happened before the words in one particular moment. There isn't one correct order.

When I say “voice,” “ask,” or “answer,” use whatever form is actually there. You can say something out loud, write it, draw, use a picture or a song, notice a sensation or urge, or just do something caring. Having little inner speech doesn't mean you must have vivid imagery instead. And a quiet mind isn't proof that you're resisting the work.

You don't have to put every feeling into words right away. Words can still help later when you're trying to work out what happened, compare explanations, or decide what to do. Plain analysis isn't automatically avoidance, and a feeling doesn't become more true just because it arrived before the explanation.

## Regulation May Come Before Dialogue

Sometimes the useful thing is just getting the charge down enough that you can work with it. If your solar plexus, abdomen, or somewhere else feels clenched and it's hard to relax into that heart-chakra love, try a slower, non-forced exhale or some gentle massage. I love using one foot to massage the other like a Yin/Yang symbol. Circular or spiral massage over the tense area can be nice too.

For deeper somatic work, you may need Shaking, tapping (Emotional Freedom Technique), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or another bottom-up approach before talking to the child is useful. I put the sequence in the roadmap below because the order matters.

[EXISTING SOMATIC THERAPY MODALITIES EMBED — UNCHANGED]

If imagery starts pulling you away from the actual room, time, or body you're in, keep your eyes open and stay with what's here. If a session leaves you functioning worse, feeling more compelled, or less oriented afterward, make it shorter and get some grounded support instead of trying to overpower your own nervous system.

### Catch the Hook Before You Interpret It

You don't always need to know yet whether it's the child, a protector, or something from the past. First catch the moment you get hooked.

Maybe your jaw tightens or your belly contracts, heat comes up, or something in you just pulls back. Then before you know it you're writing the text, reaching for a drink, trying to explain everything, or deciding what the whole relationship means.

[Pema Chödrön](https://pemachodronfoundation.org/product/taking-the-leap-book/) uses the Tibetan word *shenpa* for this—the tightening and urge that show up before the whole story has finished assembling itself.

Look around and admit, “I'm hooked.” Unless something is actually unsafe and needs action now, give it one to three breaths before you speak or do anything. Feel what's happening in the body without deciding yet what it proves. Then ask what kind of adult help would be useful right now—some warmth, some protection, or some direction. Do one small adult thing, or let the charge settle and get on with the day.

Being hooked doesn't tell you whether you're right. Something real may be happening now while old stuff is getting mixed into it, or you may be reading the situation wrong. Pausing isn't dismissing any of that. It just keeps the most activated version of you from deciding the whole case immediately.

For the next ten minutes, the question is much simpler: what keeps anybody from getting hurt, and what should probably not be said, sent, consumed, promised, or decided yet?

The meaning can wait. Later you can ask what got hit and whether there is also a real grievance in the present. Maybe an old history is getting touched; maybe there is a boundary to set, something to grieve or repair, or some care you never got.

When you start doing that, don't rewrite the experience on the way back through it. “My stomach tightened” is something you noticed. “That person is evil” is a conclusion. What did they actually do? What supports the conclusion, what doesn't, and what else could explain it? And if there were literal words in your head at the time, those were part of the event. Words you find afterward can still help you understand it, but they're your translation of what happened.

This isn't an endurance test. One breath can be enough. If turning inward starts making you less oriented, less functional, or more compelled, stop and get support from outside yourself.

### Also Look Outward

Being triggered doesn't automatically mean you're wrong about what's happening. Look at the other person too. Can they hear disagreement without punishing you for it? Can they look at their own behavior, take responsibility, and make room for what happened to you? Or do these conversations keep ending with you carrying their feelings and abandoning your own position?

[Lindsay Gibson's work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) on emotional immaturity is useful here because it gets you out of endless guessing about motives. Watch what somebody repeatedly shows they can actually do. Sometimes the answer is not another better explanation from you.

One bad conversation isn't enough to diagnose somebody, either. They can disagree with you, need time, or set a boundary of their own without being emotionally immature. And sometimes you simply won't know whether they can't respond differently, won't, or just can't right now. You can still know what you can't rely on today. Let their behavior change your assessment, not another promise. You also don't need to keep collecting danger as evidence before protecting yourself.

Guilt is lousy evidence by itself. You may have hurt somebody and need to repair it. You may also be about to abandon your own position just to make their disappointment stop, and those two things can happen in the same argument.

Before the next interaction, decide what a realistic win even is. Mutual understanding would be nice, but sometimes the useful outcome is simply conveying the information, saying no, or ending the exchange without forty minutes of defending yourself. You don't have to make somebody understand before you act.

Here the Witness can notice what's happening inside while the Protector watches what's actually happening between you and the other person. With both in view, the Guide can decide the next sane move.

### Keep the Draft. Edit the Response. Care for the Writer.

Write the response you actually want to give—or just say it in your head. Don't send it yet.

Now edit it as somebody who is on your side and still wants to be fair. Keep whatever protest, responsibility, request, or boundary is actually valid. “Better” doesn't necessarily mean nicer. Maybe you send it. Maybe you say less, wait, or don't respond. “I need some time. I'll give you a fuller response tomorrow” can be enough if you can really keep that promise. If protection is needed now, don't postpone it because you haven't finished the exercise.

Then go back to the first draft and pay attention to the person who wrote it. What were they feeling? What did they need somebody to understand, protect, reassure, or help with? That first response isn't automatically childish. It may contain the most mature protest in the room. Edit the communication without turning against its author. Sending a good message and actually caring for the one who wrote the angry version are two different jobs.

### When More Processing Becomes the Hook

You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be real while you're also checking for the hundredth time whether you've finally grieved it correctly. Deal with safety and whatever practical thing needs doing, but another round of analysis isn't automatically another round of care.

Ask what the processing is actually doing. Are you feeling the thing more honestly or seeing something you hadn't seen, enough that it changes a decision or how you respond? Or are you asking the same question again because you need the answer to feel certain this time? Real grief and real practice can revisit familiar ground. Repetition by itself doesn't mean the child brought you a new request.

If it's a checking loop, let the thought sit there without debating it or trying to make it disappear. You don't have to wait until it feels completely solved before going back to the person, activity, or life you chose. Caring for the child doesn't require calling a meeting every time the mind produces a sentence.

Before repeating the same exercise again, ask what it is supposed to help and what would actually look different if it were working. You can leave a session calmer and full of insight while the original problem isn't changing. If the method keeps giving you no useful contact—or mostly makes you monitor yourself more while daily life gets worse—don't just do it harder. Keep what really helps and try another way of meeting the same need.

The exercises here should not become a ritual you have to complete before you're allowed to live.
